Loudspeaker sound intensity: final form!

Picking up where we left off: more than two months after part 1, part 2 of sound visualization is finally here. Writing takes not just time but the right mood and frame of mind. Today it felt right, and I’ve just published a paper on sound visualization, so I got straight to it.

1. Developments in the 20th century

1. World War I and World War II

In the 20th century, with progress in industry and technology, sound visualization should have entered a period of rapid growth, with Arnold and Crandall of AT&T and Western Electric in the US standing out in particular. But World War II took priority over all science and technology, and acoustics was mainly put to work in military communications.

2. Early scan-based sound visualization

Only after the war, in the 1960s, did sound visualization regain attention and start developing again. Winston Kock imaged sound by letting a microphone’s electrical signal vary the brightness of a lamp, which was recorded by a camera.

3. Cymatics

Cymatics comes from the Greek word for wave (the physics kind of wave. What were you thinking? ?_?). The term was coined by Hans Jenny in the 1960s. A huge Chladni fanboy, he obsessively reproduced Chladni’s experiments and took them further. Some have questioned how scientific his methods were, but that doesn’t diminish his contribution to sound visualization.

Sound visualization with cymatics

* Video source: http://nigelstanford.com/Cymatics/?s=youtube&p=Chladni

4. Holographic interferometry

As early as the 1940s, Dennis Gabor proposed a method for recording both the amplitude and the phase of a wavefront, but it wasn’t put to real use until the 1960s. By measuring at different positions on a hologram plane, the sound field can be reconstructed.

2. Sound visualization today

From the 1960s on, with huge advances in sensor technology, algorithms and computing power, sound visualization entered its heyday. Many methods emerged, and they fall roughly into two groups: direct and indirect. Let’s take a closer look.

1. Acousto-optic mapping

The principle: in a region of high pressure, light travels faster, and in a region of low pressure, slower. A laser interferometer measures the resulting phase changes in the laser beam, which records the sound field and makes it possible to visualize it.

2. Acoustic holography

Like many other techniques in acoustics, acoustic holography is an import: it came over from optics in the 1980s. Simply put, it reconstructs information about the source from measurements of the sound field.

More recently, near-field acoustic holography (NAH) has allowed measurements in the near field, reconstructing the sound field more faithfully. Because it measures so close to the source, NAH captures evanescent waves, which decay exponentially with distance. Evanescent waves are not limited by wavelength, which gives NAH its high spatial resolution. But because the measurements must be made in the near field, theoretical propagation models often fail to reflect the actual test environment, which limits how well NAH works.

3. Beamforming

The acoustic telescope (or acoustic antenna), the forerunner of beamforming, was first proposed by Billingsley in 1974. With advances in data acquisition systems, algorithms and hardware, beamforming took off and is now in wide use. The simplest and earliest form is delay-and-sum beamforming, which adjusts the delays of the microphone signals to scan the reconstruction plane and locate sources.

Beamforming owes its fame among the general public to the term “acoustic camera.” The catchy name, plus real-time imaging, made for great word of mouth.

Beyond basic beamforming, many improved algorithms followed, such as MUSIC, MVDR, deconvolution and, popular over the past decade, compressive sensing: yes, yet another technique imported into acoustics. Spatial resolution has improved step by step, but beamforming has its limitations too. Because it measures in the far field and is affected by the test conditions, beamforming can locate sources but cannot reconstruct them.

4. Direct mapping

The ideal method is to put the sensor right next to the source and measure there. Besides needing no propagation model and giving accurate results, it lets you get close to the surfaces of all sorts of odd sources and hear their truest sound.

The methods mentioned so far are all indirect. In the words of M. Kac, they

Attempt to obtain what is not available based on what is available.

So wouldn’t everyone be happy if everything were available?

In a later article, I’ll go into the advantages of the Microflown particle velocity sensor: it can measure in the near field, effectively suppresses background noise and can be used to calculate sound intensity, giving you first-hand information straight from the source. So grab the probe and go explore all the weird and wonderful sources you’re curious about!

The Scan&Paint technique grew out of the Microflown intensity probe. In short, you scan with the sensor and then build an image. The Microflown probe combines a particle velocity sensor and a MEMS microphone. Sweep it around the target source and it measures velocity and pressure directly, from which the intensity is calculated and a map of the sound field drawn.

Microflown’s Scan&Paint 3D system

Below are source maps obtained by scanning the surface of a loudspeaker with a Microflown probe. Scan&Paint 2D has only a one-dimensional velocity sensor, so its maps are two-dimensional. Scan&Paint 3D has three orthogonal velocity sensors, so besides the calculated intensity values, it also gives the direction of the intensity.

In automotive NVH, Scan&Paint 3D can locate sources inside the cabin. In the figure below, the car is idling and the cabin is scanned with the 3D probe. You can see that engine noise leaks in mainly between the windshield and the dashboard, and between the right-hand door and the dashboard. Note that this plot is for 50–63 Hz; to use beamforming in this frequency range, the array would have to be huge. So the advantage of direct mapping is obvious.

Besides locating sources, scanning the cabin and visualizing the results helps to study the sound field and the cabin’s resonant modes, which supports the design of car audio systems.

3. Conclusion

Another history series finally polished off.

Sound visualization is an effective tool for understanding sources and sound fields, and for solving sound problems, noise problems above all. Acoustics may be the science of the ear, but people tend to trust what they see. As the Chinese saying goes, what the ear hears is illusory; what the eye sees is real. So why not use ears and eyes together? Next, I’ll turn to the listening side of acoustics: auralization. Only this time, the “illusory” is the virtual of virtual reality and virtual acoustics; in Chinese, the two are the same word.

References

[1] Fernandez Comesana, Daniel. Scan-based sound visualisation methods using sound pressure and particle velocity. Diss. University of Southampton, 2014.

[2] Heilmann, D. W. I. G., Doebler, D., & Boeck, M. (2014, October). Exploring the limitations and expectations of sound source localization and visualization techniques. In INTER-NOISE and NOISE-CON Congress and Conference Proceedings (pp. 4003–4011).

[3] C. M. Hutchins, K. A. Stetson, and P. A. Taylor, “Classification of free plate tap tones by holographic interferometry. The acoustics of violin plates,” Catgut Acoustical Society Newsletter, vol. 16, pp. 15–23, 1971.
